summary:
As part of our project, we have created an advanced navigation aid for exploring Mars on foot. This solution consists of two complementary tools. First, an interactive first-person 3D visualization that provides a realistic immersion in the terrain. Second, an interactive 2D map that offers an overview to help plan and ensure safe travel across the planet.

By combining these two tools, the system helps astronauts choose the safest and most optimal route. The 2D application simulates all potential hazards and provides useful information about the route (true colors of Mars, color by elevation (topography), geology, radiation, and markers). It also accurately calculates the amount of oxygen required.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

This project is a two-part Martian exploration platform combining a real-scale 3D interactive reconstruction of Mars in Unity and a web-based Surface Exploration Simulator (Live Simulator), both built from official NASA and USGS datasets:

  • 3D Global Reconstruction (Unity): Users start with an orbital view of Mars textured with the Viking MDIM 2.1 mosaic and shaped by MOLA altimetry. A menu lets them select from 10 historical missions (Perseverance, Curiosity, Opportunity, Spirit, Viking 1 & 2, Pathfinder, Phoenix, Zhurong, and InSight), triggering a smooth camera cutscene down to the landing site where they can walk across procedurally generated 3D terrain (.raw heightmaps sliced from MOLA). An A-powered GPS* calculates routes between any two latitude/longitude coordinates, displaying the path in blue on both the globe and surface.
  • Web Mission Simulator (Jezero & Gale Craters): Built as an offline-capable, single-file Leaflet web app, it embeds pre-processed JSON/Base64 CTX Digital Terrain Models, USGS geological maps, and real rover traverses (Perseverance’s 708 waypoints; Curiosity’s sols 3–5073 route). It dynamically simulates surface radiation (calibrated via Curiosity’s RAD instrument) and astronaut life-support consumption ($\text{O}_2$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and metabolic energy per NASA BVAD and OCHMO NASA-STD-3001 standards) across terrain slopes.

What benefits does it have?

  • Unified Data: Centralizes elevation (MOLA/CTX), orbital imagery, geology, climate, radiation, and metabolic metrics into one platform instead of separate NASA portals.
  • Pre-Mission Training: Lets explorers "walk" routes over authentic relief to scout slopes, obstacles, and points of interest while modeling physiological and radiological constraints.
  • Global & Site-Specific Coverage: Pairs deep analysis at Jezero and Gale craters with free-coordinate exploration across the entire planet.

What is the intended impact of the project?

It democratizes planetary science for students, educators, and the public by transforming raw NASA/USGS mission data into an intuitive, hands-on experience.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Engines & Languages: Unity (C#) for 3D rendering, procedural meshes, UI Canvas, and A* pathfinding; Python for climate data; HTML/CSS/JavaScript with Leaflet for the web simulator.
  • Processing & Data: GDAL (gdal_translate) to slice MOLA .raw elevation patches; JSON/Base64 encapsulation for offline web execution; NASA/USGS MOLA, Viking MDIM 2.1, CTX DTMs, USGS geological maps, Mars Climate Database, NASA/JPL MMGIS traverses, RAD radiation data, and NASA BVAD/OCHMO standards.

How is your project creative?

It features seamless space-to-surface camera cutscenes, 100% script-generated terrain meshes without Unity Terrain objects, a planetary free-coordinate GPS with an astronaut-style HUD minimap, and dual-scale EVA modeling.

What factors did your team consider?

We prioritized scientific accuracy (real planetary scale and calibrated physical models), performance (localized terrain patches in Unity and zero-latency embedded data on the web), ergonomics (non-overlapping GPS/mission UI), and scalability (one universal walking system for the entire planet).
